title: What To Do With All This Nuclear Waste?
summary: Josh and Chuck (with the show's co-host voice, labeled iHeart Intro in the transcript) explain how nuclear waste is produced and managed. They cover reactor fuel assemblies, spent fuel pools and canals, dry casks, the Yucca Mountain repository and its cancellation, interim storage sites in New Mexico and Texas, Finland's Onkalo deep geological repository, low-level and transuranic waste (including the Waste Isolation Pilot Plant), decommissioning and discharge of cooling water, recycling and reprocessing startups such as Oklo, security concerns about plutonium and dirty bombs, transmutation, and vitrification. The episode ends with a listener mail request about inmate counsel in Louisiana as a possible short episode.

entities.name: If Anyone Builds It, Everyone Dies

segments.title: Opening banter and Simpsons nuclear waste jokes
segments.summary: Hosts joke about the Simpsons' glowing green rod and describe nuclear waste as solid metal fuel pellets, then introduce the topic.

segments.title: Scale of nuclear waste per person
segments.summary: Discussion of how little nuclear waste is produced compared with total nuclear power use, the hockey-puck comparison, and the roughly 90,000 tons in the US.

segments.title: How nuclear reactors work and spent fuel pools
segments.summary: Explains that reactors boil water to drive turbines using fuel assemblies kept underwater, and that spent fuel is moved by canal to spent fuel pools where it cools for years.

segments.title: Fuel replacement and cooling
segments.summary: Reactors replace about a third of fuel assemblies every year and a half to two years; spent fuel stays in pools for two to five years because exposure to air could cause fires and release cesium-137.

segments.title: Dry cask storage and Surry
segments.summary: Describes the move from pools to dry casks, the first US dry storage at Surry in Virginia in 1986, cask design with inert gas and concrete, and the roughly 100-year design life.

segments.title: Yucca Mountain and interim storage in New Mexico and Texas
segments.summary: Covers the NRC review of consolidated interim storage sites, the Yucca Mountain project cancelled in 2010 after Nevada opposition, and the capacity and filling timeline of the New Mexico site.

segments.title: Onkalo deep geological repository in Finland
segments.summary: Describes Finland's Onkalo repository about 1,430 feet underground, copper-coated canisters, bentonite clay sealing, capacity for 3,000 canisters, and the debate over how long waste stays dangerous.

segments.title: Low-level and transuranic waste
segments.summary: Explains that high-level waste is about 3 percent of volume but most radioactivity, low-level waste is buried in shallow sites in four US locations, and transuranic defense waste goes to WIPP.

segments.title: Nuclear semiotics and back catalog
segments.summary: Mention of the earlier nuclear semiotics episode and the show's back catalog, plus the 2014 episode on fusion reactors.

segments.title: WIPP salt storage and plant decommissioning
segments.summary: Describes WIPP's salt layer seal and decommissioning, where only about 1 percent of plant concrete is radioactive and spent fuel remains on site after shutdown.

segments.title: Cooling water discharge and dilution
segments.summary: Discusses how contaminated cooling water is filtered and diluted before release into oceans, rivers, or lakes, with doubts about whether it is clean enough; mentions Simpsons three-eyed fish.

segments.title: Recycling spent fuel, Oklo, and security concerns
segments.summary: Covers recycling spent fuel to extract usable uranium, Oklo's Oak Ridge plans and claim of recovering 94 percent of uranium, DOE pilot program, security risks like dirty bombs and plutonium theft, and concerns about AI-backed startups; mentions the book If Anyone Builds It, Everyone Dies.

segments.title: Transmutation, vitrification, and MOX fuel
segments.summary: Explains transmutation of radioactive waste in particle accelerators, vitrification trapping waste in glass or ceramic logs, and MOX fuel recycling, with the point that separating the high-level fraction would greatly shrink the problem.

segments.title: Listener mail: inmate counsel in Louisiana
segments.summary: Listener Kelly Gizmondi, a Louisiana lawyer, asks for an episode on inmate counsel and the book The Jailhouse Lawyer by Calvin Duncan; the hosts agree it could be a short episode.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts thank the listener and give the email address; iHeartRadio credit.
